hook: That middle option on the menu often is not meant for you.

blocks.narration: That middle option on the menu often is not meant for you. It is a decoy, designed to push you toward the expensive one.
blocks.visual: Minimal surreal 3D clay popcorn buckets in three sizes on a pastel counter, soft studio light

blocks.narration: Imagine a small popcorn for four dollars and a large for eight. Lots of people would happily pick the small one.
blocks.visual: Two clay buckets glow, a small figure reaching toward the small one

blocks.narration: Now the theater adds a medium for seven fifty. Suddenly the large, just fifty cents more, looks like an amazing deal.
blocks.visual: A medium bucket pops in between, and a sparkle appears over the large bucket

blocks.narration: Hardly anyone buys the medium. It is not supposed to sell. Its only job is to make the large look smart.
blocks.visual: The medium bucket sits alone with a tiny spotlight and a dusty cobweb

blocks.narration: Psychologists call this the decoy effect, or asymmetric dominance. It was first described by marketing researchers back in nineteen eighty-two.
blocks.visual: Clay research papers flutter onto a pastel desk

blocks.narration: It works because we judge options by comparing them to each other, not by asking what we actually need.
blocks.visual: A clay balance scale weighs the buckets against each other, ignoring a tiny figure

blocks.narration: Once you know it, you will spot it in subscription plans, phone storage tiers, coffee sizes, and software pricing pages everywhere.
blocks.visual: Clay phone, coffee cups, and pricing cards line up in tidy rows

blocks.narration: Next time, ask yourself which option you would choose if the decoy vanished. Comment the sneakiest decoy you have ever spotted.
blocks.visual: The medium bucket disappears in a puff, and the figure calmly picks the small one

captions.hook_line: That middle option on the menu isn't for you. It's a decoy 🍿
captions.body: The decoy effect, described by researchers Huber, Payne and Puto in 1982, happens when adding a clearly worse option makes another option look better. Example prices here are illustrative.

youtube_title: The Decoy Option Designed to Make You Spend More
